character.centerRule: Solomon remains the center where the bounded source materially develops his identity, action, reign, literary association, or remembered legacy. Parallel witnesses and attributed voices retain their own genre and evidence boundaries.

phases.orientation: Solomon enters the story through birth, promise, preparation, contested succession, and the consolidation of David’s throne.
phases.title: Promise and succession

phases.orientation: A request for discernment develops into judgment, administration, learning, prosperity, and military wealth.
phases.title: Wisdom and royal order

phases.orientation: Labor, materials, measurements, craftsmanship, palace construction, and the Temple’s furnishings make royal building visible.
phases.title: Building the house

phases.orientation: The ark enters the Temple, glory fills it, Solomon prays, sacrifices are offered, and the people celebrate.
phases.title: Ark, prayer, and dedication

phases.orientation: God answers the dedication while Solomon’s projects, labor system, fleet, and exchanges with Hiram continue.
phases.title: Divine response and royal works

phases.orientation: The queen of Sheba, royal wealth, tribute, Psalm 72, and Psalm 127 place Solomon’s fame beside ideals of justice and dependent labor.
phases.title: Reputation, wealth, and royal ideals

phases.orientation: Foreign marriages, other gods, adversaries, Jeroboam, death notices, and later memory expose the reign’s fracture.
phases.title: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign

phases.orientation: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song, and Wisdom preserve distinct voices and editorial claims associated with Solomon.
phases.title: Works bearing Solomon’s name

phases.orientation: Later Scripture remembers Solomon through warning, genealogy, splendor, wisdom, Temple critique, and the division inherited by Rehoboam.
phases.title: Later memory and aftermath

character.throughline: The trail moves from birth, succession, wisdom, and administration through Temple construction and dedication, international splendor, divided loyalty, death, attributed works, and later canonical memory.

leftEvidence.title: Solomon is born and named Jedidiah

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Bathsheba bears a son named Solomon; the LORD loves him and sends the name Jedidiah through Nathan.
points.right: David identifies the future Temple site, gathers foreign workers and materials, tells Solomon that the promised son of rest will build, and commands Israel’s leaders to help.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: David comforts Bathsheba, and the child survives after the death narrated immediately before him.
points.right: Solomon receives a task tied to inherited preparation, peace, courage, wisdom, covenant obedience, skilled workers, and public support.

compares.posture: Solomon’s birth-name and David’s later building charge place personal divine love beside a public royal task.

rightEvidence.title: David prepares and charges Solomon to build

compares.tension: The child is loved before any achievement, while the builder’s success is later spoken with covenant conditions.
compares.title: Loved child and promised builder

leftEvidence.title: David presents Solomon before Israel

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: David names Solomon as the chosen builder and calls him to know God, serve wholeheartedly, and seek God.
points.right: David gives Solomon plans, weights, divisions, and a pattern received by the Spirit, then points to workers and leaders.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The gathered leaders hear that royal and Temple succession are bound together.
points.right: Solomon receives detailed inherited preparation rather than inventing the Temple alone.

compares.posture: David’s public charge names Solomon as chosen; the next scene gives the plans and people needed for the work.

rightEvidence.title: David gives plans and assignments

compares.tension: Choice does not eliminate dependence on inherited revelation, skill, and communal labor.
compares.title: Chosen builder and inherited pattern

leftEvidence.title: Leaders give willingly for the house

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: David gives from royal and personal treasure and invites leaders to consecrate themselves by giving.
points.right: The assembly worships, offers sacrifices, and makes Solomon king a second time; Solomon sits on the LORD’s throne.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Leaders, officers, and the people rejoice because gifts are offered willingly.
points.right: Israel obeys Solomon, and leaders pledge allegiance.

compares.posture: The people’s giving prepares the house while public worship and allegiance establish Solomon’s rule.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon is enthroned before the LORD

compares.tension: Communal devotion supports both sacred construction and royal succession.
compares.title: Willing gifts and public enthronement

leftEvidence.title: Adonijah acts as king

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Adonijah exalts himself, gathers supporters, sacrifices, and excludes Solomon while Nathan and Bathsheba alert David.
points.right: David orders Solomon placed on the royal mule and anointed; the city rejoices while Adonijah’s gathering dissolves.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Court factions assemble around competing claims before David publicly decides.
points.right: Solomon begins by sparing Adonijah conditionally and sending him home.

compares.posture: Adonijah declares himself king, while Solomon receives David’s command, priestly anointing, and the city’s acclaim.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon is anointed at Gihon

compares.tension: Both men gather public signs, but only one succession is authorized by the reigning king.
compares.title: A claimed throne and a public anointing

leftEvidence.title: David gives Solomon a final charge

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: David commands courage and covenant obedience, recalls the promise, and gives instructions concerning Joab, Barzillai’s sons, and Shimei.
points.right: Adonijah is executed after requesting Abishag, Abiathar is removed, Joab is killed, Benaiah is elevated, and Shimei dies after breaking an oath.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Solomon inherits both the covenant horizon and David’s unfinished political accounts.
points.right: Bathsheba, priests, soldiers, and rivals are drawn into the consolidation.

compares.posture: David’s last instructions frame the executions and removals that establish Solomon’s throne.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon consolidates the throne

compares.tension: Covenant obedience and dynastic violence are handed to Solomon in the same succession.
compares.title: Inherited charge and violent consolidation

leftEvidence.title: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon makes a marriage alliance with Egypt and loves the LORD, yet sacrifices at high places before the Temple is built.
points.right: At Gibeon, God invites a request; Solomon asks for discernment to judge the people, and receives wisdom plus riches and honor.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Royal devotion, foreign alliance, and unfinished worship arrangements coexist.
points.right: Solomon responds to the dream with worship at Jerusalem and a feast for servants.

compares.posture: The opening assessment praises Solomon’s love for the LORD but notes alliance and high places before the dream at Gibeon.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon asks for a listening heart

compares.tension: A wise request emerges within choices the narrative has already qualified.
compares.title: Qualified devotion and a humble request

leftEvidence.title: A judgment reveals royal wisdom

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon hears two women claim one living child and uses a threatened division to expose protective love.
points.right: Officials, priests, secretaries, commanders, household managers, and twelve district governors are named.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: One woman yields her claim to save the child; Israel fears the king’s God-given wisdom.
points.right: The kingdom is sustained through offices, territorial districts, and monthly provision.

compares.posture: One dispute displays personal judgment; the official list displays the structure required for national rule.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon orders the kingdom

compares.tension: Royal wisdom works through both human perception and administrative systems, with different risks.
compares.title: Discernment in a case and order across a kingdom

leftEvidence.title: Abundance and provision sustain the court

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Judah and Israel are numerous and secure while Solomon rules, receives tribute, maintains a large table, and keeps horses.
points.right: God gives Solomon breadth of mind; he speaks proverbs and songs and studies plants and animals.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: District officers supply the royal household without failing their assigned months.
points.right: People from every nation and kings come to hear his wisdom.

compares.posture: The provision report measures royal scale, while the wisdom report measures sayings, songs, observation, and listeners.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon’s wisdom reaches the nations

compares.tension: Prosperity and learning both extend Solomon’s fame, but neither guarantees covenant faithfulness.
compares.title: Courtly abundance and breadth of mind

leftEvidence.title: Chronicles remembers the request for wisdom

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon and the assembly worship at Gibeon; God invites a request and grants wisdom, knowledge, wealth, and honor.
points.right: Solomon gathers chariots and horsemen, makes silver common, and imports horses and chariots through royal traders.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The public setting and tabernacle equipment frame the royal request.
points.right: Royal agents conduct an international military and luxury trade.

compares.posture: Chronicles moves from Solomon’s request for wisdom to concentrated chariots, horses, silver, and trade.

rightEvidence.title: Chariots, gold, and trade accumulate

compares.tension: The granted gift is followed by practices that resemble Torah’s royal warnings.
compares.title: Wisdom requested and power accumulated

leftEvidence.title: Solomon contracts for cedar and labor

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon and Hiram arrange timber, food, skilled work, forced labor, and stone preparation for the Temple.
points.right: Solomon builds the house with chambers and carefully prepared stone; God speaks about dwelling among Israel if Solomon obeys.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Israelites, Sidonians, carriers, quarrymen, and supervisors sustain the project.
points.right: Builders shape the structure while the narrator dates it from the exodus.

compares.posture: The first scene exposes diplomatic and labor arrangements; the second interrupts measurements with a conditional promise of presence.

rightEvidence.title: The Temple rises under a covenant word

compares.tension: A sacred project can be carefully built while its covenant meaning remains dependent on obedience.
compares.title: The labor system and the word within the house

leftEvidence.title: Wood, gold, and cherubim fill the interior

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The inner rooms are lined, carved, overlaid, partitioned, and furnished with large cherubim.
points.right: Solomon spends thirteen years on royal buildings, including the Forest of Lebanon, judgment hall, residence, and a house for Pharaoh’s daughter.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Craft work creates an enclosed sacred space without a carved image of God.
points.right: Royal life receives a larger and longer construction program than the Temple.

compares.posture: Temple interiors and royal buildings display different scales, materials, and durations within one construction era.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon builds his palace complex

compares.tension: The narrative juxtaposes seven years for the house with thirteen years for royal buildings without giving a direct verdict.
compares.title: The inner sanctuary and the palace complex

leftEvidence.title: Huram fashions the Temple vessels

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Huram makes pillars, capitals, the sea, stands, basins, and bronze work; Solomon supplies gold furnishings and brings David’s dedicated gifts.
points.right: Solomon requests a skilled worker and timber from Huram, acknowledges that heaven cannot contain God, and numbers resident foreigners for labor.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: A named craftsman and many workers make the material instruments of worship.
points.right: Foreign laborers, carriers, cutters, and supervisors are assigned to the project.

compares.posture: Kings names Huram’s finished works; Chronicles emphasizes the planning, foreign skill, and labor force that precede them.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon prepares a great house

compares.tension: Temple beauty depends on people and systems whose contribution can disappear behind royal credit.
compares.title: Named craftsmanship and organized labor

leftEvidence.title: The house is built on Mount Moriah

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Chronicles locates the Temple at Moriah and describes dimensions, gold, cherubim, veil, and pillars.
points.right: The altar, sea, basins, lampstands, tables, courts, utensils, and doors are made in prescribed metals and placements.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Solomon builds at a place tied to David’s preparation and an earlier appearance.
points.right: Huram-abi and Solomon complete a large inventory for Temple service.

compares.posture: One account gives the site and enclosing forms; the next inventories the instruments placed into service.

rightEvidence.title: The bronze and gold work is completed

compares.tension: Place, symbol, and equipment create a worship environment without containing God.
compares.title: Sacred place and ordered service

leftEvidence.title: The ark enters and glory fills the house

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon assembles Israel, priests bring the ark, a cloud fills the house, and Solomon blesses the assembly.
points.right: Solomon praises covenant faithfulness, asks the promise to David to continue, and asks God to hear prayers directed toward the house.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Priests withdraw because of the cloud; the king interprets fulfillment of the promise to David.
points.right: The king stands before the altar and addresses God before the assembly.

compares.posture: The cloud fills the house, then Solomon says heaven cannot contain God and asks heaven to hear prayers directed there.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon asks the uncontainable God to hear

compares.tension: Divine presence is genuinely located without becoming confined.
compares.title: Glory in the house and prayer to heaven

leftEvidence.title: Solomon prays across guilt, disaster, exile, and foreigners

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The prayer asks God to judge, forgive, teach, send rain, hear foreigners, support battle, and restore exiles.
points.right: Solomon blesses the assembly, urges wholehearted obedience, offers many sacrifices, and celebrates fourteen days.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Israel, individuals, foreigners, armies, and captives appear as possible petitioners.
points.right: The people depart joyful for the goodness shown to David and Israel.

compares.posture: The prayer imagines sin, drought, defeat, and exile; the feast celebrates fulfilled promise and abundant sacrifice.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon blesses the people and holds the feast

compares.tension: Dedication holds future failure in view without canceling present gratitude.
compares.title: Anticipated failure and present joy

leftEvidence.title: Singers and trumpeters accompany the glory

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The ark enters, singers and trumpeters praise God’s goodness and covenant love, and the cloud fills the house.
points.right: Solomon blesses Israel, recounts David’s desire and his own building, kneels with spread hands, and asks God to hear.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Priests cannot stand to minister because of the glory.
points.right: The king publicly interprets dynasty, city, house, covenant, and prayer.

compares.posture: Corporate music accompanies glory, while Solomon’s kneeling prayer interprets place, dynasty, and hearing.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon kneels before the assembly

compares.tension: Public spectacle and spoken dependence are distinct responses to the same dedication.
compares.title: One sound and one kneeling king

leftEvidence.title: Petitions move toward exile and the anointed king

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon asks for judgment, forgiveness, rain, relief, foreigner inclusion, victory, and return from exile, ending with an appeal for the anointed.
points.right: Fire consumes the offerings, glory fills the house, and the people bow while musicians and sacrifices accompany the festival.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The prayer anticipates failure and asks that confession and return be heard.
points.right: Priests cannot enter; Israel praises enduring covenant love and celebrates.

compares.posture: Solomon’s petitions culminate in an appeal for God’s resting place; fire and glory answer when he finishes.

rightEvidence.title: Fire falls and the people worship

compares.tension: The dramatic answer confirms acceptance without answering every future petition in advance.
compares.title: Prayer rises and fire descends

leftEvidence.title: God answers Solomon with promise and warning

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: God says the house is consecrated and the dynasty will endure with faithful walking, but apostasy will bring removal and ruin.
points.right: God promises to hear humble repentance, establishes the conditional dynasty, and warns that abandonment will make the house an astonishment.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The future nations may ask why the land and house became a warning.
points.right: Prayer, seeking, turning, forgiveness, healing, and covenant loyalty are linked.

compares.posture: Kings and Chronicles preserve overlapping promises and warnings while Chronicles expands the language of humble prayer and healing.

rightEvidence.title: Chronicles expands the answer to the prayer

compares.tension: Both make the accepted house conditional, but their remembered emphases differ.
compares.title: Two accounts of the divine response

leftEvidence.title: Cities, labor, and a fleet extend the reign

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon exchanges cities with Hiram, builds fortified centers, levies forced labor from subject peoples, and sends a fleet for gold.
points.right: Solomon rebuilds cities, assigns forced labor, moves Pharaoh’s daughter, orders priestly service, and develops a fleet with Huram.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Hiram disputes the cities; Canaanite descendants labor; Israelites hold military and administrative roles.
points.right: Residents, Israelites, priests, Levites, officers, sailors, and the royal household occupy distinct roles.

compares.posture: Both surveys name cities, labor, officers, worship arrangements, and maritime trade after dedication.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon’s projects and worship order continue

compares.tension: Ordered achievement and coercive labor remain close together even when the accounts select different details.
compares.title: Royal projects in Kings and Chronicles

leftEvidence.title: The queen of Sheba tests Solomon

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The queen asks hard questions, sees wisdom and royal order, praises the LORD, exchanges gifts, and receives what she desires.
points.right: The queen tests Solomon, praises his wisdom and Israel’s God, gives gifts, and receives royal generosity.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Her breath leaves her at the scale of what she hears and sees.
points.right: Temple ascent and royal order become part of what she sees.

compares.posture: Both tellings preserve hard questions, astonishment, praise, and gifts; Chronicles highlights the Temple ascent and justice.

rightEvidence.title: Chronicles retells the queen’s visit

compares.tension: The same visit supports overlapping but not identical portraits of royal wisdom.
compares.title: The queen’s visit in two accounts

leftEvidence.title: Gold, shields, throne, chariots, and horses accumulate

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon receives enormous gold, makes shields and a throne, acquires luxury goods, and multiplies chariots and imported horses.
points.right: Gold, shields, throne, vessels, ships, gifts, chariots, and horses display Solomon’s international reach.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Merchants, kings, traders, and royal agents feed a concentrated display of wealth and power.
points.right: Kings seek his wisdom and bring annual gifts.

compares.posture: Both inventories display gold, throne, trade, chariots, horses, and international attention.

rightEvidence.title: Chronicles gathers the wealth report

compares.tension: The reports celebrate splendor while the accumulated features echo royal limits elsewhere in Scripture.
compares.title: The wealth report in Kings and Chronicles

leftEvidence.title: A royal prayer asks for justice and peace

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The psalm asks God to give the king justice, defend the poor, crush oppression, extend peace, receive tribute, and bless all nations.
points.right: The queen asks hard questions, sees wisdom and royal order, praises the LORD, exchanges gifts, and receives what she desires.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The needy, poor, oppressed, kings, nations, and the whole earth appear within the royal horizon.
points.right: Her breath leaves her at the scale of what she hears and sees.

compares.posture: Psalm 72 measures rule through defense of the poor and peace, while the queen sees wisdom, servants, worship, and wealth.

rightEvidence.title: The queen of Sheba tests Solomon

compares.tension: International admiration is not the same measure as the psalm’s justice for the vulnerable.
compares.title: The prayed-for king and the admired king

leftEvidence.title: A Solomon psalm limits human building

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The psalm says building, guarding, anxious labor, and family security depend on the LORD’s gift.
points.right: Solomon and Hiram arrange timber, food, skilled work, forced labor, and stone preparation for the Temple.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Builders, watchmen, laborers, sleepers, parents, and children are placed under divine provision.
points.right: Israelites, Sidonians, carriers, quarrymen, and supervisors sustain the project.

compares.posture: Psalm 127 denies self-securing labor, while Kings names the large workforce behind Solomon’s Temple project.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon contracts for cedar and labor

compares.tension: The Solomon-associated psalm relativizes the achievement most closely associated with his reign.
compares.title: Unless the LORD builds and the labor system that built

leftEvidence.title: Solomon marries Pharaoh’s daughter

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Solomon makes a marriage alliance with Egypt and loves the LORD, yet sacrifices at high places before the Temple is built.
points.right: Solomon loves many foreign women, builds high places, and follows other gods; the LORD announces that the kingdom will be torn.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Royal devotion, foreign alliance, and unfinished worship arrangements coexist.
points.right: The king’s wives turn his heart, and covenant warning becomes dynastic judgment.

compares.posture: The early assessment says Solomon loved the LORD with a qualification; the later judgment says other loves turned his heart.

rightEvidence.role: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign
rightEvidence.title: Solomon’s heart turns toward other gods

compares.tension: The narrative traces a real beginning in devotion without treating it as irreversible.
compares.title: Love for the LORD and a divided heart

leftEvidence.role: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign
leftEvidence.title: Hadad and Rezon become adversaries

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The LORD raises adversaries from Edom and Aram whose histories reach back through David’s wars and regional violence.
points.right: Ahijah tears a new garment, gives ten pieces to Jeroboam, explains Solomon’s breach, and offers Jeroboam a conditional house.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Hadad escapes as a child, returns from Egypt, and Rezon establishes rule in Damascus.
points.right: Jeroboam receives a promise, while Solomon seeks to kill him and he flees to Egypt.

compares.posture: Hadad and Rezon arise through regional histories, while Jeroboam receives a prophetic share of Solomon’s kingdom.

rightEvidence.role: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign
rightEvidence.title: Ahijah gives ten pieces to Jeroboam

compares.tension: Judgment works through different human actors whose own aims and responsibilities remain intact.
compares.title: External adversaries and an internal rival

leftEvidence.role: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign
leftEvidence.title: Solomon dies after forty years

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The book of Solomon’s acts is cited; Solomon dies and is buried, and Rehoboam reigns.
points.right: Prophetic records are cited; Solomon dies after forty years and Rehoboam succeeds him.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The death notice closes the reign without repeating wisdom, wealth, or apostasy in summary.
points.right: Nathan, Ahijah, and Iddo are named as sources around the reign.

compares.posture: Kings closes after apostasy and adversaries; Chronicles closes after glory while citing different prophetic records.

rightEvidence.role: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign
rightEvidence.title: Chronicles closes Solomon’s reign

compares.tension: The same death formula ends two differently shaped memories of the reign.
compares.title: Two endings to Solomon’s reign

leftEvidence.role: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign
leftEvidence.title: Sirach praises and indicts Solomon

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Sirach remembers peace, wisdom, songs, wealth, sexual surrender, defilement, divided kingdom, and a surviving remnant.
points.right: Solomon loves many foreign women, builds high places, and follows other gods; the LORD announces that the kingdom will be torn.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Solomon becomes an example of both extraordinary gift and damaging failure.
points.right: The king’s wives turn his heart, and covenant warning becomes dynastic judgment.

compares.posture: Kings narrates the divided heart; Sirach turns the reign into praise followed by moral warning.

rightEvidence.role: Divided loyalty and the end of the reign
rightEvidence.title: Solomon’s heart turns toward other gods

compares.tension: Later memory intensifies judgment while retaining admiration for wisdom and fame.
compares.title: The fracture narrated and remembered

leftEvidence.title: Proverbs opens with Solomon’s name

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The collection identifies proverbs of Solomon and states aims of wisdom, instruction, justice, prudence, knowledge, and fear of the LORD.
points.right: A new heading introduces sayings about wise children, unjust treasure, hunger, diligence, and harvest.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Learners, youths, wise people, and interpreters are invited into instruction.
points.right: Family response, economic conduct, divine provision, and work are compressed into paired lines.

compares.posture: Proverbs 1 names the whole work’s educational purpose; Proverbs 10 introduces a distinct Solomonic collection.

rightEvidence.title: A Solomonic collection turns to short sayings

compares.tension: Both bear Solomon’s name while their literary functions and forms differ.
compares.title: A book heading and a collection heading

leftEvidence.title: Hezekiah’s men copy Solomon’s proverbs

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: A heading says Judah’s officials copied additional proverbs of Solomon, followed by sayings about hidden matters and royal presence.
points.right: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, names vapor, cycles, forgotten generations, and the grief of wisdom.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Later scribes preserve and arrange material attributed to an earlier king.
points.right: A royal first-person voice applies the heart to know wisdom and madness.

compares.posture: Hezekiah’s officials copy Solomonic sayings, while Ecclesiastes constructs a son-of-David royal speaker.

rightEvidence.title: The Teacher tests royal wisdom

compares.tension: Association with Solomon can arise through editorial transmission or literary persona rather than one simple authorship model.
compares.title: Later copying and a royal literary voice

leftEvidence.title: The Teacher tests royal wisdom

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, names vapor, cycles, forgotten generations, and the grief of wisdom.
points.right: The Teacher is described as wise, careful, and truthful; the final voice warns about books and directs fear of God and judgment.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: A royal first-person voice applies the heart to know wisdom and madness.
points.right: A narrator evaluates the Teacher’s work and addresses the reader beyond the Teacher’s first-person quest.

compares.posture: The opening launches the royal search; the ending describes, commends, and bounds the Teacher’s words.

rightEvidence.title: An epilogue evaluates the Teacher

compares.tension: The work allows a searching voice and a framing voice to remain distinguishable.
compares.title: The Teacher speaks and the epilogue evaluates

leftEvidence.title: The Song bears Solomon’s name

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The superscription names the Song of Songs as Solomon’s, while a woman’s voice immediately speaks of desire, fragrance, chambers, and joy.
points.right: The collection identifies proverbs of Solomon and states aims of wisdom, instruction, justice, prudence, knowledge, and fear of the LORD.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: The opening speaker and companions enter before Solomon becomes a character in the poems.
points.right: Learners, youths, wise people, and interpreters are invited into instruction.

compares.posture: The Song opens in lyric desire; Proverbs opens in instruction, justice, and fear of the LORD.

rightEvidence.title: Proverbs opens with Solomon’s name

compares.tension: Solomonic attribution does not imply a single genre, speaker, or purpose.
compares.title: Two works bearing Solomon’s name

leftEvidence.title: A royal voice prefers wisdom to wealth

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: The speaker prays and receives understanding, choosing wisdom over scepters, riches, health, beauty, and light.
points.right: The prayer recalls creation and human rule, confesses weakness, asks wisdom to come from God’s throne, and links salvation to divine counsel.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Wisdom arrives with other goods and becomes an unfailing treasure shared with others.
points.right: The chosen builder of a Temple confesses that even a complete human is nothing without wisdom.

compares.posture: One passage values wisdom above royal goods; the other asks wisdom to come from God’s throne for rule and Temple building.

rightEvidence.title: The speaker asks wisdom to share the throne

compares.tension: The royal voice treats wisdom as both chosen treasure and received gift.
compares.title: Wisdom preferred and wisdom requested

leftEvidence.title: Nehemiah uses Solomon as a warning

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Nehemiah confronts Judeans over foreign marriages and cites Solomon as a beloved king led into sin by foreign women.
points.right: Matthew traces David’s line through the wife of Uriah to Solomon, then through Rehoboam.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Postexilic family and language practices are judged through remembered royal failure.
points.right: Solomon is remembered inside a genealogy that retains the shadow of David’s act against Uriah.

compares.posture: Nehemiah remembers Solomon’s sin; Matthew remembers Solomon in the line from David toward Jesus.

rightEvidence.title: Solomon enters Jesus’ genealogy

compares.tension: Later Scripture can preserve moral warning and genealogical importance without letting either erase the other.
compares.title: Solomon as warning and ancestor

leftEvidence.title: Jesus compares lilies with Solomon’s glory

points.label: Solomon-relative action
points.left: Jesus points to lilies clothed by God and says Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of them.
points.right: Jesus refuses a demanded sign except Jonah’s and says the queen of the south will judge the generation because she came to hear Solomon’s wisdom.

points.label: Response and consequence
points.left: Anxious hearers are directed from royal splendor to ordinary creation and divine care.
points.right: Solomon’s wisdom becomes a witness against those who resist a greater presence.

compares.posture: Jesus makes Solomon lesser than lilies clothed by God and lesser than the one present before the sign-seeking generation.

rightEvidence.title: Jesus speaks of one greater than Solomon

compares.tension: Royal glory and wisdom remain memorable precisely as subordinate comparison points.

edges.basis: Solomon’s birth-name and David’s later building charge place personal divine love beside a public royal task. The child is loved before any achievement, while the builder’s success is later spoken with covenant conditions.
edges.label: Loved child and promised builder

edges.basis: David’s public charge names Solomon as chosen; the next scene gives the plans and people needed for the work. Choice does not eliminate dependence on inherited revelation, skill, and communal labor.
edges.label: Chosen builder and inherited pattern

edges.basis: The people’s giving prepares the house while public worship and allegiance establish Solomon’s rule. Communal devotion supports both sacred construction and royal succession.
edges.label: Willing gifts and public enthronement

edges.basis: Adonijah declares himself king, while Solomon receives David’s command, priestly anointing, and the city’s acclaim. Both men gather public signs, but only one succession is authorized by the reigning king.
edges.label: A claimed throne and a public anointing

edges.basis: David’s last instructions frame the executions and removals that establish Solomon’s throne. Covenant obedience and dynastic violence are handed to Solomon in the same succession.
edges.label: Inherited charge and violent consolidation

edges.basis: The opening assessment praises Solomon’s love for the LORD but notes alliance and high places before the dream at Gibeon. A wise request emerges within choices the narrative has already qualified.
edges.label: Qualified devotion and a humble request

edges.basis: One dispute displays personal judgment; the official list displays the structure required for national rule. Royal wisdom works through both human perception and administrative systems, with different risks.
edges.label: Discernment in a case and order across a kingdom

edges.basis: The provision report measures royal scale, while the wisdom report measures sayings, songs, observation, and listeners. Prosperity and learning both extend Solomon’s fame, but neither guarantees covenant faithfulness.
edges.label: Courtly abundance and breadth of mind

edges.basis: Chronicles moves from Solomon’s request for wisdom to concentrated chariots, horses, silver, and trade. The granted gift is followed by practices that resemble Torah’s royal warnings.
edges.label: Wisdom requested and power accumulated

edges.basis: The first scene exposes diplomatic and labor arrangements; the second interrupts measurements with a conditional promise of presence. A sacred project can be carefully built while its covenant meaning remains dependent on obedience.
edges.label: The labor system and the word within the house

edges.basis: Temple interiors and royal buildings display different scales, materials, and durations within one construction era. The narrative juxtaposes seven years for the house with thirteen years for royal buildings without giving a direct verdict.
edges.label: The inner sanctuary and the palace complex

edges.basis: Kings names Huram’s finished works; Chronicles emphasizes the planning, foreign skill, and labor force that precede them. Temple beauty depends on people and systems whose contribution can disappear behind royal credit.
edges.label: Named craftsmanship and organized labor

edges.basis: One account gives the site and enclosing forms; the next inventories the instruments placed into service. Place, symbol, and equipment create a worship environment without containing God.
edges.label: Sacred place and ordered service

edges.basis: The cloud fills the house, then Solomon says heaven cannot contain God and asks heaven to hear prayers directed there. Divine presence is genuinely located without becoming confined.
edges.label: Glory in the house and prayer to heaven

edges.basis: The prayer imagines sin, drought, defeat, and exile; the feast celebrates fulfilled promise and abundant sacrifice. Dedication holds future failure in view without canceling present gratitude.
edges.label: Anticipated failure and present joy

edges.basis: Corporate music accompanies glory, while Solomon’s kneeling prayer interprets place, dynasty, and hearing. Public spectacle and spoken dependence are distinct responses to the same dedication.
edges.label: One sound and one kneeling king

edges.basis: Solomon’s petitions culminate in an appeal for God’s resting place; fire and glory answer when he finishes. The dramatic answer confirms acceptance without answering every future petition in advance.
edges.label: Prayer rises and fire descends

edges.basis: Kings and Chronicles preserve overlapping promises and warnings while Chronicles expands the language of humble prayer and healing. Both make the accepted house conditional, but their remembered emphases differ.
edges.label: Two accounts of the divine response

edges.basis: Both surveys name cities, labor, officers, worship arrangements, and maritime trade after dedication. Ordered achievement and coercive labor remain close together even when the accounts select different details.
edges.label: Royal projects in Kings and Chronicles

edges.basis: Both tellings preserve hard questions, astonishment, praise, and gifts; Chronicles highlights the Temple ascent and justice. The same visit supports overlapping but not identical portraits of royal wisdom.
edges.label: The queen’s visit in two accounts

edges.basis: Both inventories display gold, throne, trade, chariots, horses, and international attention. The reports celebrate splendor while the accumulated features echo royal limits elsewhere in Scripture.
edges.label: The wealth report in Kings and Chronicles

edges.basis: Psalm 72 measures rule through defense of the poor and peace, while the queen sees wisdom, servants, worship, and wealth. International admiration is not the same measure as the psalm’s justice for the vulnerable.
edges.label: The prayed-for king and the admired king

edges.basis: Psalm 127 denies self-securing labor, while Kings names the large workforce behind Solomon’s Temple project. The Solomon-associated psalm relativizes the achievement most closely associated with his reign.
edges.label: Unless the LORD builds and the labor system that built

edges.basis: The early assessment says Solomon loved the LORD with a qualification; the later judgment says other loves turned his heart. The narrative traces a real beginning in devotion without treating it as irreversible.
edges.label: Love for the LORD and a divided heart

edges.basis: Hadad and Rezon arise through regional histories, while Jeroboam receives a prophetic share of Solomon’s kingdom. Judgment works through different human actors whose own aims and responsibilities remain intact.
edges.label: External adversaries and an internal rival

edges.basis: Kings closes after apostasy and adversaries; Chronicles closes after glory while citing different prophetic records. The same death formula ends two differently shaped memories of the reign.
edges.label: Two endings to Solomon’s reign

edges.basis: Kings narrates the divided heart; Sirach turns the reign into praise followed by moral warning. Later memory intensifies judgment while retaining admiration for wisdom and fame.
edges.label: The fracture narrated and remembered

edges.basis: Proverbs 1 names the whole work’s educational purpose; Proverbs 10 introduces a distinct Solomonic collection. Both bear Solomon’s name while their literary functions and forms differ.
edges.label: A book heading and a collection heading

edges.basis: Hezekiah’s officials copy Solomonic sayings, while Ecclesiastes constructs a son-of-David royal speaker. Association with Solomon can arise through editorial transmission or literary persona rather than one simple authorship model.
edges.label: Later copying and a royal literary voice

edges.basis: The opening launches the royal search; the ending describes, commends, and bounds the Teacher’s words. The work allows a searching voice and a framing voice to remain distinguishable.
edges.label: The Teacher speaks and the epilogue evaluates

edges.basis: The Song opens in lyric desire; Proverbs opens in instruction, justice, and fear of the LORD. Solomonic attribution does not imply a single genre, speaker, or purpose.
edges.label: Two works bearing Solomon’s name

edges.basis: One passage values wisdom above royal goods; the other asks wisdom to come from God’s throne for rule and Temple building. The royal voice treats wisdom as both chosen treasure and received gift.
edges.label: Wisdom preferred and wisdom requested

edges.basis: Nehemiah remembers Solomon’s sin; Matthew remembers Solomon in the line from David toward Jesus. Later Scripture can preserve moral warning and genealogical importance without letting either erase the other.
edges.label: Solomon as warning and ancestor

edges.basis: Jesus makes Solomon lesser than lilies clothed by God and lesser than the one present before the sign-seeking generation. Royal glory and wisdom remain memorable precisely as subordinate comparison points.
edges.label: Splendor surpassed and wisdom surpassed

edges.basis: Matthew and Luke preserve the queen’s journey and Jesus’ greater claim within related but distinct narrative arrangements. Parallel witness supports the claim while preserving each Gospel’s placement and sequence.
edges.label: The greater-than-Solomon saying in two settings

edges.basis: Solomon says heaven cannot contain God while asking that prayers toward the house be heard; Stephen cites the same limit in a prophetic accusation. The builder’s own prayer provides a boundary later used to challenge confidence in the building.
edges.label: Solomon’s prayer and Stephen’s Temple critique

edges.basis: Both accounts trace the split through Rehoboam’s harsh answer to a complaint about Solomon’s service burden. Human folly, inherited policy, prophetic word, and divine purpose all remain in the event’s explanation.
edges.label: The inherited yoke and the divided kingdom

edges.basis: Kings narrates Solomon building for foreign gods; generations later Josiah destroys and defiles those sites. A private divided heart becomes a durable public landscape of worship.
edges.label: Solomon’s high places built and destroyed

edges.basis: Shishak removes treasures soon after Solomon, while Babylon later cuts up the remaining gold articles Solomon made. Royal splendor erodes in stages as covenant judgment reaches palace, Temple, and people.
edges.label: The gold work diminished and destroyed

edges.basis: The ark and cloud mark dedication; Babylonian fire and dismantling mark the city’s fall. The same house can be a real place of glory without becoming immune to covenant judgment.
edges.label: Glory fills the house and fire consumes the house

edges.basis: The dedication sends Israel away joyful; Hezekiah’s Passover is remembered as joy unmatched since Solomon. Later renewal receives Solomon’s era as a worship memory rather than merely a wealth memory.
edges.label: Solomon’s feast and Hezekiah’s renewed joy

edges.basis: The superscription associates the Song with Solomon; the procession presents Solomon as a figure seen and addressed within the poetry. Association with the work and participation inside its lyric world are different literary claims.
edges.label: Solomonic heading and Solomon inside the poem

edges.basis: The Song contrasts royal vineyard revenue with a woman’s own vineyard; Kings inventories concentrated royal treasure and power. The lyric voice asserts possession beside the same king whose reign is known for accumulation.
edges.label: Solomon’s vineyard and Solomon’s accumulated wealth

edges.basis: Chronicles narrates fire and glory; 2 Maccabees recalls Solomon’s prayer and sacrifice alongside Moses. Later memory joins traditions that the earlier dedication account keeps in its own narrative frame.
edges.label: Dedication narrated and remembered

edges.basis: Both Gospels preserve Solomon as the lesser comparison to flowers clothed by God within teaching about anxiety. Shared saying material remains embedded in distinct Gospel sequences and audiences.
edges.label: Solomon and the lilies in Matthew and Luke

edges.basis: 2 Esdras makes Solomon’s city part of Zion’s symbolic grief; Acts places his building under the claim that God is not contained by handmade houses. Later memory can honor the builder’s place in Jerusalem while refusing to equate God with the built place.
edges.label: Solomon’s city remembered and Solomon’s house bounded

edges.basis: The people give abundantly, and David interprets the wealth as God’s own before asking that Solomon’s inner loyalty match the outward provision. Resources sufficient for the house cannot supply the faithful heart required of its builder.
edges.label: Willing gifts and the prayer for a whole heart

edges.basis: Both accounts report Shishak taking Solomon’s gold shields and Rehoboam replacing them with bronze. Chronicles adds humility and partial deliverance to the material loss preserved in Kings.
edges.label: Solomon’s gold lost in Kings and Chronicles

edges.basis: Kings and Chronicles both place Manasseh’s image inside the house named to David and Solomon. The parallel accounts preserve the same defilement while Chronicles carries the story into later repentance beyond this bounded pair.
edges.label: Manasseh defiles Solomon’s house in two accounts

edges.basis: Chronicles and 1 Esdras remember Solomon’s house and ordering traditions inside Josiah’s Passover. The witnesses overlap while using distinct wording for Solomon’s written order or magnificence.
edges.label: Solomon’s Temple order in two Passover accounts

edges.basis: Kings preserves Solomon’s petitions for future worshipers; 2 Esdras cites that prayer in an argument about intercession before final judgment. The later work receives Solomon’s prayer while placing it inside a new question about the limits of prayer.
edges.label: Solomon prays and later Scripture remembers intercession

edges.basis: Proverbs names the collection’s educational aims; 4 Maccabees remembers a Solomonic saying within family formation under persecution. Later reception makes the wisdom usable in a new setting without erasing its earlier literary context.
edges.label: Solomon’s proverbs as instruction and inherited courage

topic.orientation: Follow Solomon from a loved child and contested successor through wisdom, administration, Temple building, prayer, wealth, divided loyalty, death, attributed voices, and later memory. Keep parallel accounts, literary headings, and later interpretation distinct.

pivots.description: Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song, and Wisdom preserve distinct voices and editorial claims associated with Solomon.

nodes.note: The collection identifies proverbs of Solomon and states aims of wisdom, instruction, justice, prudence, knowledge, and fear of the LORD.
nodes.title: Proverbs opens with Solomon’s name

nodes.note: A new heading introduces sayings about wise children, unjust treasure, hunger, diligence, and harvest.
nodes.title: A Solomonic collection turns to short sayings

nodes.note: A heading says Judah’s officials copied additional proverbs of Solomon, followed by sayings about hidden matters and royal presence.
nodes.title: Hezekiah’s men copy Solomon’s proverbs

nodes.note: The Teacher, son of David and king in Jerusalem, names vapor, cycles, forgotten generations, and the grief of wisdom.
nodes.title: The Teacher tests royal wisdom

nodes.note: The Teacher is described as wise, careful, and truthful; the final voice warns about books and directs fear of God and judgment.
nodes.title: An epilogue evaluates the Teacher

nodes.note: The superscription names the Song of Songs as Solomon’s, while a woman’s voice immediately speaks of desire, fragrance, chambers, and joy.
nodes.title: The Song bears Solomon’s name

nodes.note: The speaker prays and receives understanding, choosing wisdom over scepters, riches, health, beauty, and light.
nodes.title: A royal voice prefers wisdom to wealth

nodes.note: The prayer recalls creation and human rule, confesses weakness, asks wisdom to come from God’s throne, and links salvation to divine counsel.
nodes.title: The speaker asks wisdom to share the throne

nodes.note: The poem sees Solomon’s couch, warriors, carriage, crown, and wedding joy approaching from the wilderness.
nodes.title: The Song pictures Solomon’s procession

nodes.note: Solomon’s vineyard at Baal Hamon yields money through keepers, while the speaker claims direct possession of her own vineyard.
nodes.title: Solomon’s vineyard is set beside the speaker’s own

pivots.title: Works bearing Solomon’s name

pivots.description: Later Scripture remembers Solomon through warning, genealogy, splendor, wisdom, Temple critique, and the division inherited by Rehoboam.

nodes.note: Nehemiah confronts Judeans over foreign marriages and cites Solomon as a beloved king led into sin by foreign women.
nodes.title: Nehemiah uses Solomon as a warning

nodes.note: Matthew traces David’s line through the wife of Uriah to Solomon, then through Rehoboam.
nodes.title: Solomon enters Jesus’ genealogy

nodes.note: Jesus points to lilies clothed by God and says Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one of them.
nodes.title: Jesus compares lilies with Solomon’s glory

nodes.note: Jesus refuses a demanded sign except Jonah’s and says the queen of the south will judge the generation because she came to hear Solomon’s wisdom.
nodes.title: Jesus speaks of one greater than Solomon

nodes.note: Jesus calls the generation evil, names Jonah as sign, and says the queen came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon.
nodes.title: Luke pairs Solomon with Jonah

nodes.note: Stephen recalls the wilderness tent, David’s desire, Solomon’s building, and Isaiah’s claim that the Most High does not dwell in handmade houses.
nodes.title: Stephen places Solomon’s house under prophetic critique

nodes.note: Israel asks Rehoboam to lighten Solomon’s hard service; he rejects elder counsel, threatens heavier burdens, and the northern tribes revolt.
nodes.title: Rehoboam rejects the plea for lighter service

nodes.note: The assembly asks for relief from Solomon’s heavy yoke; Rehoboam follows young counselors and Israel rebels.
nodes.title: Chronicles retells the kingdom’s division

nodes.note: Josiah defiles Topheth, removes royal horses and chariots dedicated to the sun, destroys altars, and defiles the high places Solomon built for foreign gods.
nodes.title: Josiah destroys Solomon’s high places

nodes.note: Nebuchadnezzar besieges Jerusalem, removes Temple and palace treasures, and cuts up the gold articles Solomon made.
nodes.title: Babylon cuts up Solomon’s gold work

nodes.note: Babylon burns the LORD’s house and Jerusalem, breaks the bronze work, and carries its metal to Babylon.
nodes.title: The Temple is burned and bronze is carried away

nodes.note: After Rehoboam abandons the instruction, Egypt invades; leaders humble themselves, Jerusalem is spared from total destruction, and treasures and gold shields are taken.
nodes.title: Shishak takes the Temple and palace treasures

nodes.note: Judah and visiting Israelites celebrate Passover with music, teaching, confession, and extended feasting; Chronicles says Jerusalem had not known such joy since Solomon.
nodes.title: Hezekiah’s Passover recalls Solomon’s joy

nodes.note: A collected letter recalls cloud and glory at the Temple, Solomon’s dedication, fire consuming sacrifice, and Moses’ earlier offering.
nodes.title: A later Temple memory recalls Solomon’s sacrifice

nodes.note: Jesus directs disciples from anxiety to ravens and lilies, saying Solomon in all his glory was not dressed like one flower.
nodes.title: Luke remembers Solomon’s glory among the lilies

nodes.note: The interpreting angel identifies the transformed woman as Zion, the city Solomon built, and explains her grief through the Temple’s fall.
nodes.title: The mourning woman becomes Solomon’s city

nodes.note: During Rehoboam’s reign, Judah multiplies high places and Shishak takes Temple and palace treasures, including Solomon’s gold shields.
nodes.title: Kings remembers Solomon’s gold becoming bronze

nodes.note: Manasseh rebuilds high places, worships the sky’s army, practices occult rites, and installs an Asherah image in the house named to David and Solomon.
nodes.title: Manasseh places an image in the house

nodes.note: Chronicles reports Manasseh’s altars, occult practices, child sacrifice, and idol in the house tied to David and Solomon.
nodes.title: Chronicles retells Manasseh’s Temple defilement

nodes.note: Josiah orders priests and Levites for Passover, places the ark in the house Solomon built, and refers to written divisions associated with David and Solomon.
nodes.title: Josiah restores an order linked to Solomon

nodes.note: The account of Josiah’s Passover places the ark in Solomon’s house and orders Levitical service according to David’s writing and Solomon’s magnificence.
nodes.title: 1 Esdras remembers Solomon’s Temple order

nodes.note: Ezra asks whether the righteous can intercede after judgment and names Solomon among earlier figures who prayed for others in the present age.
nodes.title: Solomon’s prayer becomes an example of intercession

nodes.note: A mother remembers a father teaching Scripture and declaring a proverb of Solomon about a tree of life among examples of faithful endurance.
nodes.title: Solomon’s proverbs enter a martyr family’s memory
